name: Hydrogen
summary: Hydrogen fuels stars through nuclear fusion. A neutral atom of its most common isotope has one proton and one electron.

name: Helium
summary: Helium first revealed itself as a spectral line in sunlight. Liquid helium cools superconducting magnets to temperatures close to absolute zero.

name: Lithium
summary: Lithium is the lightest metal. Its ions move between the electrodes of rechargeable lithium-ion batteries.

name: Beryllium
summary: Beryllium combines low density with high stiffness. Thin beryllium windows transmit X-rays, and the metal forms the mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope.

name: Boron
discoveredBy: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, Louis Jacques Thénard and Humphry Davy
summary: Boron strengthens heat-resistant borosilicate glass. One of its naturally occurring isotopes, boron-10, readily absorbs neutrons.

name: Carbon
summary: Carbon can form four covalent bonds. Different arrangements of the same atoms produce diamond, graphite and graphene.

name: Nitrogen
summary: Two nitrogen atoms share a triple bond in atmospheric nitrogen. Plants generally obtain usable nitrogen through compounds such as nitrates and ammonium.

name: Oxygen
discoveredBy: Carl Wilhelm Scheele and Joseph Priestley
summary: Oxygen atoms make up most of the mass of water. Molecular oxygen also powers aerobic respiration in plants and animals.

name: Fluorine
summary: Fluorine attracts bonding electrons more strongly than any other element. Its compounds range from fluoride minerals to the polymer PTFE.

name: Neon
summary: An electric discharge through low-pressure neon produces the characteristic orange-red light of a traditional neon sign.

name: Sodium
summary: Sodium metal is soft and reactive. In table salt, sodium occurs as positively charged ions paired with chloride ions.

name: Magnesium
summary: A magnesium ion sits at the centre of each chlorophyll molecule. Magnesium metal also forms lightweight alloys.

name: Aluminium
summary: Aluminium quickly develops a protective oxide layer in air. Its low density makes it useful for aircraft structures and drink cans.

name: Silicon
summary: Pure silicon can be given precise electrical properties by introducing tiny amounts of other elements. This makes it central to computer chips and solar cells.

name: Phosphorus
summary: Phosphate groups connect the repeating units of DNA. Elemental phosphorus also has several forms, including white, red and black.

name: Sulfur
summary: Sulfur commonly forms yellow crystals containing rings of eight atoms. Much of the sulfur used by industry goes into sulfuric acid.

name: Chlorine
summary: Chlorine is a greenish-yellow gas. Chloride ions are widespread in seawater, and chlorine compounds disinfect drinking water.

name: Argon
summary: Argon makes up nearly one percent of dry air. Welders use it to keep hot metals from reacting with the atmosphere.

name: Potassium
summary: Potassium ions help nerves transmit signals. Potassium salts are also a major ingredient in agricultural fertilisers.

name: Calcium
summary: Calcium compounds build bones, shells and limestone. The metal's symbol comes from the Latin word for lime.

name: Scandium
summary: Small additions of scandium strengthen aluminium alloys. Its name honours Scandinavia, where scientists first identified it in rare minerals.

name: Titanium
summary: Titanium is strong for its weight and resists corrosion. Titanium dioxide supplies the white pigment in many paints.

name: Vanadium
summary: Vanadium strengthens steel. In a vanadium flow battery, different oxidation states of the same element store electrical energy.

name: Chromium
summary: A chromium-rich oxide film gives stainless steel much of its corrosion resistance. Chromium compounds can also produce vivid pigments.

name: Manganese
discoveredBy: Carl Wilhelm Scheele and Johan Gottlieb Gahn
summary: Manganese is a key ingredient in steelmaking. Manganese dioxide also serves as an electrode material in common batteries.

name: Iron
summary: Iron is the main ingredient of steel. In haemoglobin, individual iron ions help red blood cells carry oxygen.

name: Cobalt
summary: Cobalt compounds colour glass deep blue. The metal also appears in heat-resistant alloys and some battery cathodes.

name: Nickel
summary: Nickel helps stainless steel withstand corrosion. Nickel-based superalloys can retain strength at the high temperatures inside jet engines.

name: Copper
summary: Copper conducts electricity and is easily drawn into wire. On exposure to air and moisture, its surface can develop a green patina.

name: Zinc
summary: A zinc coating can protect steel from rust even when scratched. Zinc combined with copper forms brass.

name: Gallium
summary: Gallium melts just above ordinary room temperature. Gallium-containing semiconductors are used in LEDs and high-frequency electronics.

name: Germanium
summary: The properties of germanium matched many of Mendeleev's predictions for a missing element beneath silicon. Germanium transmits infrared light.

name: Arsenic
summary: Gallium arsenide is a semiconductor used in lasers and fast electronics. Elemental arsenic sublimes at ordinary atmospheric pressure.

name: Selenium
discoveredBy: Jöns Jakob Berzelius, Johan Gottlieb Gahn
summary: Selenium changes its electrical conductivity in light. Its compounds also serve as micronutrients in several enzymes.

name: Bromine
discoveredBy: Carl Jacob Löwig and Antoine Jérôme Balard
summary: Bromine is a reddish-brown liquid at room temperature. Its vapour gives the element its characteristic strong colour.

name: Krypton
summary: Krypton occurs in trace amounts in air. A spectral line of krypton-86 once defined the metre.

name: Rubidium
summary: Rubidium produces distinctive spectral lines and is used in compact atomic clocks. Its name refers to the deep red lines in its spectrum.

name: Strontium
summary: Strontium salts produce red colours in fireworks. Strontium atoms also provide a reference transition for optical clocks.

name: Yttrium
summary: Yttrium compounds appear in phosphors, lasers and technical ceramics. Its name comes from the Swedish village of Ytterby.

name: Zirconium
summary: Zirconium resists corrosion and absorbs relatively few thermal neutrons. Zirconium alloys surround fuel in many nuclear reactors.

name: Niobium
summary: Niobium alloys become superconducting at low temperatures. Niobium-titanium wire carries current in many MRI magnets.

name: Molybdenum
summary: Molybdenum improves the high-temperature strength of steel. Molybdenum disulfide is a solid lubricant with a layered structure.

name: Technetium
summary: Technetium was the first element produced artificially. Technetium-99m emits gamma rays used to trace processes inside the body.

name: Ruthenium
summary: Ruthenium belongs to the platinum group. Its compounds serve as catalysts, and the metal can harden platinum alloys.

name: Rhodium
summary: Rhodium helps catalytic converters break down nitrogen oxides. Thin rhodium coatings also give jewellery a bright reflective finish.

name: Palladium
summary: Palladium can absorb hydrogen into its metal lattice. It is widely used as a catalyst, including in carbon–carbon bond formation.

name: Silver
summary: Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any pure metal at room temperature. Light-sensitive silver salts underpin traditional photography.

name: Cadmium
discoveredBy: Friedrich Stromeyer and  Karl Samuel Leberecht Hermann
summary: Cadmium appears in nickel–cadmium batteries. Cadmium telluride converts sunlight into electricity in thin-film solar cells.

name: Indium
summary: Indium tin oxide conducts electricity while transmitting visible light, making it useful in touchscreens and flat-panel displays.

name: Tin
summary: Tin combines with copper to make bronze. Tin-based solders join metal components at relatively low temperatures.

name: Antimony
summary: Stibnite, an ore of antimony, supplied an ancient eye cosmetic. Antimony also hardens lead alloys.

name: Tellurium
summary: Tellurium compounds can convert temperature differences into electricity. Cadmium telluride is used in thin-film photovoltaics.

name: Iodine
summary: Iodine crystals give off violet vapour when heated. Small amounts of dietary iodine are needed to make thyroid hormones.

name: Xenon
summary: Xenon powers some ion thrusters. Although it belongs to the noble gases, it forms compounds such as xenon difluoride.

name: Caesium
summary: A transition in caesium-133 defines the SI second. Its atoms make a reproducible frequency reference for atomic clocks.

name: Barium
summary: Barium sulfate strongly absorbs X-rays and dissolves poorly in water. It provides contrast in certain X-ray examinations.

name: Lanthanum
summary: Lanthanum compounds are used in high-index optical glass. Lanthanum-containing alloys can also store hydrogen.

name: Cerium
discoveredBy: Martin Heinrich Klaproth, Wilhelm Hisinger, Jöns Jacob Berzelius
summary: Cerium can switch readily between two common oxidation states. Cerium oxide is used to polish glass and in automotive catalysts.

name: Praseodymium
summary: Praseodymium compounds can colour glass and ceramics. The metal contributes to alloys used in strong permanent magnets.

name: Neodymium
summary: Neodymium, iron and boron form powerful permanent magnets. Neodymium ions can also produce laser light in transparent crystals.

name: Promethium
discoveredBy: Charles D. Coryell, Jacob A. Marinsky, Lawrence E. Glendenin
summary: Every isotope of promethium is radioactive. Scientists identified the element among the products of uranium fission.

name: Samarium
summary: Samarium forms strong permanent magnets with cobalt. Some samarium isotopes absorb neutrons exceptionally well.

name: Europium
summary: Europium ions can emit intense red or blue light depending on their chemical environment. They are used in phosphors and security markings.

name: Gadolinium
summary: Gadolinium compounds alter magnetic resonance signals. Certain gadolinium isotopes also absorb thermal neutrons very efficiently.

name: Terbium
summary: Terbium ions produce green light in phosphors. Terbium-containing alloys can change shape in a magnetic field.

name: Dysprosium
summary: Adding dysprosium can help permanent magnets maintain their magnetism at elevated temperatures.

name: Holmium
summary: Holmium has a large magnetic moment. Holmium ions in laser crystals produce infrared light absorbed strongly by water.

name: Erbium
summary: Erbium-doped optical fibres amplify signals at wavelengths used for long-distance communications.

name: Thulium
summary: Thulium-doped laser materials emit infrared light. Thulium is one of the least abundant naturally occurring lanthanides.

name: Ytterbium
summary: Ytterbium-doped fibres generate high-power laser light. Ytterbium atoms are also used in optical atomic clocks.

name: Lutetium
discoveredBy: Carl Auer von Welsbach, Georges Urbain, Charles James
summary: Lutetium-containing crystals convert gamma radiation into flashes of light in PET scanners.

name: Hafnium
summary: Hafnium is chemically similar to zirconium but absorbs thermal neutrons much more strongly. Hafnium oxide is an insulator used in chips.

name: Tantalum
summary: Tantalum forms a thin, stable insulating oxide. This allows compact tantalum capacitors to store electrical charge.

name: Tungsten
summary: Tungsten has the highest melting point of the metals. Tungsten carbide gives cutting tools a hard, wear-resistant edge.

name: Rhenium
discoveredBy: Walter Noddack, Ida Noddack, Otto Berg
summary: Rhenium helps turbine-blade alloys withstand prolonged exposure to heat. It occurs in small amounts in some molybdenum ores.

name: Osmium
summary: Osmium is among the densest elements. Its oxide, osmium tetroxide, is used to stain structures for electron microscopy.

name: Iridium
summary: Iridium is a dense, corrosion-resistant platinum-group metal. A layer rich in iridium marks the end-Cretaceous impact in rocks around the world.

name: Platinum
summary: Platinum catalyses reactions in catalytic converters and fuel cells. Its resistance to corrosion also makes it suitable for laboratory equipment.

name: Gold
summary: Gold can be beaten into extremely thin leaf. Its resistance to oxidation helps gold-plated electronic contacts stay reliable.

name: Mercury
summary: Mercury is liquid at room temperature. It expands predictably with heat, a property historically used in thermometers.

name: Thallium
summary: Thallium can activate light emission in scintillation crystals, allowing detectors to register ionising radiation.

name: Lead
summary: Lead is dense and easy to shape. Its compounds store energy through reversible reactions in lead–acid batteries.

name: Bismuth
summary: Bismuth can grow stepped crystals with iridescent surface oxides. The metal is also used in low-melting alloys.

name: Polonium
summary: Marie and Pierre Curie identified polonium while studying radioactive ore. Its name honours Marie Curie's homeland, Poland.

name: Astatine
discoveredBy: Dale R. Corson, Kenneth Ross MacKenzie, Emilio Segrè
summary: Astatine is a short-lived radioactive halogen. Only tiny amounts occur naturally as heavier radioactive nuclei decay.

name: Radon
summary: Radon forms in natural radioactive decay chains. As a noble gas, it can escape from mineral grains into surrounding air.

name: Francium
summary: Marguerite Perey found francium among the decay products of actinium. All its isotopes are short-lived.

name: Radium
summary: Radium forms in the decay chains of heavier elements. Its name reflects the penetrating radiation that helped reveal it.

name: Actinium
discoveredBy: André-Louis Debierne and Friedrich Oskar Giesel
summary: Actinium gives its name to the actinide series. Actinium-227 occurs in the natural decay chain of uranium-235.

name: Thorium
summary: Thorium-232 decays so slowly that much of Earth's original thorium remains. Monazite is one of its mineral sources.

name: Protactinium
summary: Protactinium lies between thorium and uranium. Protactinium-231 occurs as an intermediate in the uranium-235 decay chain.

name: Uranium
summary: Naturally occurring uranium consists mostly of uranium-238. The less abundant uranium-235 can sustain a fission chain reaction with slow neutrons.

name: Neptunium
summary: Neptunium was the first element beyond uranium to be identified. It was produced by irradiating uranium with neutrons.

name: Plutonium
discoveredBy: Glenn T. Seaborg, Arthur Wahl, Joseph W. Kennedy, Edwin McMillan
summary: Plutonium-238 supplies heat for radioisotope power systems on spacecraft. Plutonium was named after Pluto.

name: Americium
discoveredBy: Glenn T. Seaborg, R. A. James, Leon O. Morgan, A. Ghiorso
summary: Americium-241 emits alpha particles. Small sealed sources of this isotope are used in ionisation smoke detectors.

name: Curium
discoveredBy: Glenn T. Seaborg, Ralph A. James, Albert Ghiorso
summary: Curium honours Marie and Pierre Curie. Curium-244 has supplied alpha particles for instruments analysing rocks on Mars.

name: Berkelium
summary: Berkelium was named for Berkeley, California. A berkelium-249 target helped researchers produce atoms of tennessine.

name: Californium
summary: Californium-252 undergoes spontaneous fission and emits neutrons. It is used as a compact neutron source.

name: Einsteinium
summary: Researchers detected einsteinium in debris from the first thermonuclear test. Its name honours Albert Einstein.

name: Fermium
summary: Fermium was identified along with einsteinium in thermonuclear-test debris. It is named after physicist Enrico Fermi.

name: Mendelevium
summary: Mendelevium was initially identified atom by atom after an einsteinium target was bombarded with alpha particles. It honours Dmitri Mendeleev.

name: Nobelium
summary: Nobelium is named after Alfred Nobel. It favours the +2 oxidation state more strongly than most other actinides.

name: Lawrencium
discoveredBy: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Joint Institute for Nuclear Research
summary: Lawrencium closes the actinide series. It honours Ernest Lawrence, inventor of the cyclotron.

name: Rutherfordium
summary: Rutherfordium starts the fourth transition-metal series. Experiments on small numbers of atoms have compared its chemistry with that of hafnium.

name: Dubnium
summary: Dubnium is named for Dubna in Russia. Its group places it below tantalum, whose chemistry helps guide experiments with individual dubnium atoms.

name: Seaborgium
summary: Seaborgium honours chemist Glenn Seaborg. Experiments have studied volatile compounds of this short-lived group 6 element.

name: Bohrium
summary: Bohrium honours Niels Bohr. Researchers study its chemical behaviour by making and detecting very small numbers of atoms.

name: Hassium
summary: Hassium takes its name from the German state of Hesse. Experiments with hassium tetroxide connect its chemistry to that of osmium.

name: Meitnerium
summary: Meitnerium honours Lise Meitner. Its first identified nucleus was made by fusing iron and bismuth nuclei.

name: Darmstadtium
summary: Darmstadtium was first produced in Darmstadt, Germany. Its short-lived nuclei are identified through their radioactive decay chains.

name: Roentgenium
summary: Roentgenium honours Wilhelm Röntgen, who discovered X-rays. Its position beneath gold places it in group 11.

name: Copernicium
summary: Copernicium honours Nicolaus Copernicus. Experiments with individual atoms have explored how this group 12 element interacts with gold surfaces.

name: Nihonium
summary: Nihonium takes its name from Nihon, a Japanese name for Japan. RIKEN researchers identified it through the decay of nuclei made from zinc and bismuth.

name: Flerovium
discoveredBy: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
summary: Flerovium lies below lead in group 14. Researchers produced it by bombarding plutonium with calcium ions.

name: Moscovium
discoveredBy: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
summary: Moscovium belongs to group 15 and honours the Moscow region. Its first reported nuclei were produced from americium and calcium.

name: Livermorium
discoveredBy: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
summary: Livermorium honours Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Its place in group 16 puts it below polonium.

name: Tennessine
discoveredBy: Dubna, Livermore, Oak Ridge and Vanderbilt collaboration
summary: Tennessine was synthesised using a berkelium target and a calcium beam. It occupies the group 17 position below astatine.

name: Oganesson
discoveredBy: Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
summary: Oganesson completes period seven. Only a few atoms have been detected, leaving its bulk properties experimentally unknown.

name: Ununennium
summary: Ununennium is the systematic placeholder for element 119. A neutral atom is predicted to begin an eighth electron shell, placing it below francium.

name: Unbinilium
summary: Unbinilium is the systematic placeholder for element 120. Calculations put two electrons in its eighth shell, in the position below radium.
